Trump Appointees Asked a Federal Cybersecurity Agency to Secretly Acquire a Voting Machine — and Hack It
items.summary: A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it. The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request. The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. “My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.” The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA.

items.title: Defense contractors in two NATO allies hacked in recent Russia-linked campaign
items.summary: Russian state-linked hackers targeted a naval shipbuilder, a military aircraft engine manufacturer and a law enforcement agency in two NATO countries in a recent espionage campaign, researchers have found. The attacks were attributed to APT28, a hacking group linked to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, according to cybersecurity firm Symantec. The researchers did not identify the two NATO countries or the organizations targeted, saying only that the victims were located in Europe. The hackers used a recently discovered backdoor known as Hookedge to gain access to victims' systems, steal credentials and gather information about their networks. The malware was first documented in August by Recorded Future's Insikt Group. In one attack against a naval shipbuilder, the hackers gained access after an employee opened a malicious Microsoft Word document received as an email attachment in July. The attackers subsequently explored the company's internal network and attempted to steal login credentials. Over the following week, the hackers repeatedly returned to a compromised computer and deployed a previously undocumented tool designed to decrypt and execute malicious code directly in the computer's memory. The tool's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

items.title: Tech Giants Block eMudhra Certificates Tied to 8 Compromised Keys
items.summary: Google, Mozilla, Apple, and the Go programming language project blocked certificates signed with eight compromised certificate authority (CA) keys in a widening response to an incident that could allow attackers to impersonate any legitimate website or service. The affected keys were associated with intermediate certificates issued by Indian CA eMudhra. Six were used to issue TLS certificates for websites while the other two were used for code signing. The blocks are designed to prevent browsers and applications from trusting fraudulent digital certificates that attackers might issue using the compromised keys, reducing the risk of website impersonation and the potential interception of encrypted communications. However, the protections do not automatically extend to all users and applications. Mozilla, Google, and Apple have distributed blocks through their respective certificate-revocation mechanisms, while applications built with Go must be rebuilt using patched versions to receive the fix. Other software may also require updates, depending on how they manage certificate trust.

items.title: ROMULUS: Analysis of a New Multi-Payload ClickFix Delivery Platform
items.summary: We recently reported how cybercriminals use ClickFix to deliver malware loaders that are then leveraged to deploy final payloads such as RATs or ransomware on victim machines. On September 28, Huntress reported a campaign that adds a new link to that common attack chain: threat actors abused ChatGPT’s Custom GPTs that were programmed to present to victims links to pages serving the ClickFix lures that are then used to deliver loaders. The server hosting the ClickFix script in that campaign was 96.62.224[.]81 and the trojanized software used to sideload malware included a Canon application (ISOSimple.msi) and Stardock DeElevation (IconEdit2Turb.msi). While investigating an independent incident, we noticed the exact same malware being delivered via another server, 86.109.75[.]7. Beyond that, the new server hosted a panel called ROMULUS. Investigating that panel, we identified a new multi-payload shared ClickFix delivery platform. Here, we detail how ROMULUS was used in two delivery chains. The identity of the operator behind the platform and common ownership of the final malware families are unknown. ROMULUS may be a privately operated panel, a commercial cybercriminal delivery service, an affiliate framework, or software that has been copied between operators. Notably, we have no evidence that this panel is related to the RomulusLoader reported by Proofpoint as being used by the Silver Fox threat actor earlier this year.

items.title: ClickFix Attackers Exploit Siemens Software Center Flaw to Deploy Remote Access Trojan
items.summary: Siemens has addressed a DLL sideloading vulnerability impacting Siemens Software Center that it said has been exploited in ClickFix attacks. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v4 score: 8.4), could allow an attacker to place a specially-crafted DLL in a directory the application searches, resulting in execution of malicious code with the same privileges as the affected service. "The affected application loads dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from an uncontrolled search path," Siemens said in an advisory. "This could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application." The issue has been patched in version 4.0.9.8. Huntress Labs researcher Jose Oregon has been credited with discovering and reporting the shortcoming. In a separate alert, Siemens said attackers have abused a genuine copy of Siemens Software Center with a valid signature and placed their own crafted DLL ("archive.dll") next to it to trigger the execution of malicious code.

items.title: The journey of a paper unicorn: adventures inside a modern warehouse
items.summary: Imagine you’ve ordered a small paper unicorn from an online marketplace. You clicked “Buy”, received a cheerful notification, and expect a courier to bring the box tomorrow. If the unicorn is delayed by a day, it will be annoying but not catastrophic: an apology, a discount promo code — and the incident is forgotten. Now let’s multiply one late unicorn by several hundred thousand orders. Packages start heading to the wrong cities. The website shows an item is in stock, even though the required bin is empty. Conveyors stop, boxes get stuck between floors, the cargo piles up with no freight manifest. Trucks line up at the gates, and every minute of downtime turns into blown schedules, support tickets, fines, and lost sales. It is at exactly this scale that a cyberincident in a warehouse becomes a problem for the entire business. A modern warehouse is no longer just a big building with shelving. It is a tightly interconnected hybrid system: web applications, radio channels, and an automated factory. Physical processes here depend on data, and errors in data have very physical consequences.

items.title: Nikkei discloses third data breach in a month, 1.8M records exposed
items.summary: Nikkei Inc. disclosed a new data breach, the third in about a month, that exposed 1.83 million personal information records. The Japanese giant says subsets of the data contained personally identifiable information and other sensitive details, but most records contained no identifying info. The company said that 150,000 records contained at least one of the following data types: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in 120,000 records. The remaining 1.68 million records contain no identifiers, the company said, and no credit card information was exposed. Nikkei Inc. is a major Japanese business news and financial information group, owner of Financial Times, the country’s largest business-focused media company. The company employs over 10,100 people and has an annual revenue of $2.5 billion (¥393.8 billion). According to a notice Nikkei published late last week, hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within its network during the early morning hours of October 7.

items.title: CVE-2026-106173 Deep-Dive: FortiSIEM gRPC Path Traversal File Write RCE
items.summary: On 13 October 2026, Fortinet published a security advisory for a critical vulnerability affecting their FortiSIEM product. The vulnerability, CVE-2026-106173, allows for an arbitrary file write by abusing an issue in a gRPC service. Horizon3 is no stranger to the FortiSIEM. We’ve disclosed several critical vulnerabilities through the years that you can catch up on. All of our prior research has involved the same component, the phMonitor service which listens on port tcp/7900. This latest advisory details a new service that we had never looked at, a gRPC service on port tcp/27918. Given our familiarity and the intrigue of a new service to look at we dove in. Looking at the listening services on the FortiSIEM, we find that phQueryMaster is bound to tcp/27918. The phQueryMaster service stands the gRPC server up in grpcNotificationServer::run(). The listen port comes from the command_port config value (7918), which is passed through phSecureUtils::getGrpcPort() and mapped to tcp/27918; the address is built as [::]:27918, so the service binds every interface.

items.title: Xerj Console API Authentication Bypass Leads to Unauthorized Credential Minting
items.summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: None, CVEs: CVE-2026-97406, Summary: An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Xerj Console API allows sessions to bypass passkey-backed requirements during token issuance. By exploiting this flaw, an attacker with an existing valid token can create independent, persistent successor credentials directly through the console API. This allows the attacker to maintain access and potentially escalate privileges within the Xerj ecosystem, even if the initial token is revoked.

items.title: Qilin and INC Ransomware Groups Exploit Palo Alto Networks Flaw to Bypass MFA
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has disclosed that it's continuing to observe exploitation of a now-patched security flaw impacting PAN-OS and Prisma Access by ransomware actors. The activity relates to CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw that could be exploited by bad actors to set up unauthorized VPN connections. It was patched by Palo Alto Networks in May 2026 and was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CSIA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026. "Ransomware operators exploiting CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka INC)," Unit 42 researchers said in an update shared on Monday. The development comes days after ReliaQuest said it detected both Qilin and Settra ransomware groups actively exploiting the flaw in financially-motivated attacks. According to Unit 42, the threat actors are weaponizing the flaw to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, and then bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session

items.title: PHP warns admins of two critical flaws, emergency patches coming tomorrow
items.summary: The PHP security team is warning administrators to prepare for emergency security updates tomorrow to address two critical vulnerabilities, as information about the flaws has reportedly leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. PHP powers many websites and web applications, including content management systems, e-commerce platforms, and custom web services. In an advisory published Tuesday, the PHP development team announced that it plans to release security updates on Wednesday, October 21, at 14:00 UTC (10:00 AM Eastern), to address two vulnerabilities, each rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0. The PHP security team also sent a notice to its ANNOUNCE mailing list, urging administrators to prepare to install the security updates as soon as they become available. "We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild," the PHP security team warned. The developers have not disclosed any technical details about the vulnerabilities, including which PHP versions are affected, how they can be exploited, or which releases will contain fixes.However, security researchers at watchTowr told BleepingComputer that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are remote code execution (RCE) flaws believed to affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8.

items.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
items.summary: Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model. Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited. We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines. With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.
